div.head: Hn com 3
div.ab: Et si amodo exurgat placitum de diuisione terrarum uel de preocupatione, si est inter dominicos barones meos, tractetur placitum in curia mea.
Et si amodo exurgat placitum de divisione terrarum vel de preocupatione, si est inter barones meos dominicos, tractetur placitum in curia mea.
And if henceforth a case arises concerning the division or occupation of lands—if it is between crown barons of mine, the case shall be dealt with in my court.
div.note: Added October 2026 from Robertson pp. 286–287 (text and translation); Liebermann’s text added from Gesetze I p. 524, October 2026 (two independent readings of the page images)

Tenentes in capite, Kronlehnsträger. Die curia mea steht unter dem König als Gerichtsherrn, und unter ihm oder dem Oberrichter oder einem Königsrichterkolleg als Richter. Auch wo sie in letzterem Falle in der Provinz tagt, geniesst sie das Vorrecht, recognitio durch Geschworene anzuwenden; dieses fehlt dem anderen zwar öffentlichen und ebenfalls bisweilen ‘königlich’ heissenden, aber nicht zentralen, sondern lokalen Gerichte unter dem lokalen Kronbeamten (meist Sheriff), obwohl auch der damals noch, selbst bloss in dieser Eigenschaft, iusticia regis heissen kann

Tenentes in capite, tenants-in-chief of the Crown. The curia mea stands under the king as lord of the court, and under him or the chief justiciar or a bench of royal justices as judge. Even where, in the latter case, it sits in the provinces, it enjoys the privilege of employing recognitio by jurors; this privilege is lacking in the other court — public, it is true, and likewise sometimes called ‘royal’, but local rather than central — under the local Crown official (usually the sheriff), although he too, even merely in that capacity, could at that time still be called iusticia regis
